children.title: Belt Conveyor Operation
Coal Conveying System – Complete System Understanding
children.content: Thermal Power Plant | Coal Handling Plant | Pre-Site Induction Course

children.title: How to Use This Course
children.content: This course is designed to build your mental picture of the Coal Handling Plant's belt conveyor system before you set foot on the physical site. Think of it as downloading the entire system into your mind so that when you arrive, you recognise what you see, understand why it exists, and know where the dangers are. This is a context and awareness course only. It does not teach you how to start, stop, or operate any equipment. You must never attempt any operational action independently without formal training and authorisation from the plant management. After completing this course you will be able to walk around a Coal Handling Plant, identify every major component of the belt conveyor system, understand its role in power generation, and — most importantly — recognise hazardous zones and behaviours that could injure you or others.

children.title: What You Will Learn in This Course
children.content: ✓ Understand the role of the conveyor system in continuous fuel supply to the boiler. ✓ Identify all major conveyor components and understand what each one does in the system. ✓ Visualise how coal travels from the unloading point (wagon tippler) all the way to the boiler bunker. ✓ Understand the mechanism of motion, load carrying, and tension balance on a belt conveyor. ✓ Recognise how capacity limits affect system stability and plant performance. ✓ Develop awareness of high-risk zones such as transfer points, drive pulleys, and rotating parts. ✓ Understand how upstream systems like the wagon tippler directly influence conveyor behaviour.

children.title: Purpose of the Belt Conveyor System
children.content: The belt conveyor is the continuous coal transport pipeline inside the plant — like the bloodstream of the power plant. A thermal power plant burns coal to generate steam, which drives a turbine, which spins a generator to produce electricity. The entire generation cycle depends on one simple but critical requirement: a continuous, uninterrupted supply of coal to the boiler . That is exactly what the belt conveyor system does. It is the internal transportation network that moves coal — hundreds or thousands of tonnes per day — from the point where it is received (the wagon tippler / track hopper) to the coal bunkers located above the boilers. From the bunkers, coal flows down to the pulverisers (mills) that grind it into powder for combustion. Coal Mine / Railway Wagon BELT CONVEYOR SYSTEM (CHP) ← This Course → Coal Bunker & Pulveriser Boiler (Combustion) Turbine & Generator Coal-to-electricity conversion chain — Belt Conveyor is Stage 2 If the belt conveyor stops for any reason — mechanical failure, blockage, power trip, misalignment — coal stops moving. Within minutes, the bunker level drops. Within hours, boiler load has to be reduced. If not restored quickly, the entire generating unit may shut down, causing a loss of hundreds of megawatts from the grid. That is the direct consequence of this system failing. In a typical 500 MW coal-fired unit, the conveyor system must deliver approximately 250–300 tonnes of coal per hour continuously. Any interruption has an immediate, measurable cost — both financial and to the reliability of the power supply.

children.title: System Flow Integration – End-to-End View
children.content: Wagon Tippler → Hopper → Feeder → Conveyor → Transfer Points → Coal Bunker → Boiler. The conveyor is not isolated — it is one link in a synchronised chain. Before you can understand the conveyor itself, you need to visualise the complete material flow — the journey coal takes from the moment it arrives at the plant to when it reaches the boiler. Think of it like a factory assembly line: every station depends on the one before it, and supplies the one after it. RAILWAY WAGON (Coal Source) Arrival point WAGON TIPPLER (Unloading) ~20–25 min/wagon TRACK HOPPER (Buffer) Coal storage pit FEEDER / CRUSHER (Sizing) Controls feed rate BELT CONVEYOR BC-1 (This Course) Primary conveying TRANSFER TOWER (High-risk zone) BC-1 → BC-2 COAL BUNKER (Final Buffer) Above the boiler BOILER (Combustion) ⚠ CRITICAL DELIVERY ZONE Transfer Tower + Bunker filling = high-risk area Coal Flow Direction → Each station is dependent on the previous — disruption at any point affects the entire chain

children.title: Understanding Each Stage
children.content: Stage | What Happens Here | Consequence if Disrupted ; Railway Wagon | Coal-loaded wagons arrive from the mine via rail. Each wagon carries 60–80 tonnes. | No coal input — entire downstream system starves. ; Wagon Tippler / Track Hopper | Wagon is inverted or coal falls through a grated pit. Coal drops into the hopper below. | Feed is interrupted — hopper level drops, feeder starves. ; Track Hopper / Surge Hopper | Acts as a buffer storage. Absorbs variation in wagon unloading rate. Feeds the conveyor steadily. | Overflow if feed is too fast; starvation if empty. ; Feeder / Crusher | Controls the rate at which coal is loaded onto the conveyor. May include a crusher to reduce lump size. | Overload or underload on conveyor; blockages if lumps are too large. ; Belt Conveyor BC-1 | Carries coal horizontally or at an incline to the transfer tower or directly to the bunker. | Entire downstream coal supply stops. ; Transfer Tower | Junction point where coal moves from one conveyor to another (BC-1 to BC-2). Contains a chute to guide coal. | Spillage, blockage, or coal misdirection. ; Coal Bunker | Large overhead storage silo (capacity 8–12 hours of operation). Continuously fed from conveyor above. | Bunker starves → boiler load reduction → unit outage. ; Boiler | Coal from bunker is pulverised and fired. Steam drives the turbine-generator. | Power generation stops. The belt conveyor is not an isolated machine . It is one critical link in a chain. An imbalance at any point — too much coal, too little coal, wrong size coal — travels downstream and amplifies. A senior engineer thinks of the entire chain simultaneously, not just the conveyor belt in front of them.

children.title: Conveyor Components & Layout
children.content: A moving belt supported and driven across a structured path — like a moving staircase carrying coal instead of people. Before you can work safely near a belt conveyor, you must be able to name every component, point to it, and describe its function . On a real plant, supervisors will test this knowledge before allowing you near the equipment. Below is a systematic walkthrough of every major component. TAIL Tail Pulley DRIVE PULLEY Head/Drive Pulley CARRYING STRAND (Coal on top) Return Strand (empty belt going back) COAL LOAD Carry Idlers Return Idler Take-up (Tension) MOTOR + GEARBOX ↓ Feed Point (From Hopper) → Belt Travel Direction → Scraper Belt Cross-Section (Troughed Configuration) Centre Roll Wing Roll Wing Roll COAL ← Belt (Troughed) → Trough angle: typically 20°–35° Troughing increases carrying capacity vs flat belt 20–35°

children.title: 🔴 Belt
children.content: The belt is the actual carrying medium — the surface on which coal rests and moves. It is made of multiple layers: rubber covers on top and bottom, with reinforcing fabric plies (nylon, polyester, or steel cords) in between. The belt forms a continuous loop — the top strand carries coal forward; the bottom (return) strand travels empty back to the start. A typical CHP belt is 800–1400 mm wide and can be hundreds of metres long. The belt edge is sharp when damaged. The belt surface can drag anything that contacts it. Never stand on or reach over a moving belt.

children.title: 🔵 Drive Unit (Motor + Gearbox + Drive Pulley)
children.content: This is the power source of the conveyor. An electric motor (typically 110–500 kW in a CHP) drives a gearbox that reduces speed and increases torque. The gearbox output shaft is connected to the drive pulley (also called the head pulley). The belt wraps around this pulley, and friction between the pulley surface and the belt drives the entire system. The drive pulley is always at the discharge (head) end. Pinch point between belt and drive pulley. Extremely high force — instantly fatal if contacted. Must always have a fixed guard.

children.title: 🟡 Idlers
children.content: Idlers are the support rollers that keep the belt in shape and prevent it from sagging under the weight of coal. They are spaced every 1–1.5 metres along the top (carry) strand. Carry idlers are usually mounted in a 3-roll troughing configuration to form a trough shape. Return idlers support the empty belt on the return path and are usually flat or slightly tilted. Idlers rotate freely, reducing friction on the belt. Failed (seized) idlers can cause friction, heat, and fire. They also cause belt misalignment. A spinning idler can trap cloth or fingers.

children.title: ⚪ Tail Pulley
children.content: Located at the loading (start) end of the conveyor. The tail pulley is a plain pulley — it does not drive the belt. Its role is simply to act as the return point where the belt loops back. The feed point (where coal drops from the hopper/feeder) is usually just after the tail pulley. The tail pulley is also where belt tension is lowest, making slippage in this region less dangerous — but still a pinch hazard.

children.title: 🟣 Take-up System
children.content: The belt, like any loop under load, must be kept at the correct tension — not too tight, not too loose. If tension is too low, the belt slips on the drive pulley. If too high, bearings and structure are overloaded. The take-up system maintains this tension automatically. In a gravity take-up , a weighted carriage pulls the tail pulley backward using gravity. In a screw take-up , the tail pulley position is adjusted manually. In heavy-duty conveyors, an automatic hydraulic or winch-type take-up is used.

children.title: 🟤 Feed Point (Loading Zone)
children.content: This is where coal is loaded from the hopper or feeder onto the belt. The feed point includes impact idlers (heavier-duty rollers to absorb the impact of falling coal) and skirt boards (rubber or steel side walls that contain the coal on the belt as it is loaded and prevent spillage at the edges). The alignment and height of the drop point critically affects belt loading quality. Spillage is highest at feed points. Wet or fine coal can also block the skirt boards, causing pressure on the belt edge.

children.title: 🟠 Scrapers & Belt Cleaners
children.content: After coal is discharged at the head pulley, a thin layer of fine coal adheres to the belt surface and carries back on the return strand. This is called carryback . Scrapers are blades pressed against the belt surface (at the head pulley and along the return path) to remove this carryback. Without effective scrapers, carryback falls off along the return path, causing spillage, dust, and idler fouling everywhere under the belt.

children.title: 🔷 Structure, Walkways & Guards
children.content: The conveyor is mounted on a steel frame (truss or box structure) that keeps everything aligned and at the correct height. Walkways run alongside for inspection. Nip guards are fitted at all pulley-belt contact points. Emergency pull cords (emergency stop cables) run the full length of the conveyor — pulling the cord anywhere on the conveyor stops it immediately. These are life-saving devices and must never be bypassed. If you see a guard removed or a pull cord damaged, report it immediately. These are mandatory safety devices.

children.title: Functional Mechanism of Conveying
children.content: Friction-driven continuous loop — the motor grips the belt through the drive pulley; the belt carries coal through friction between coal and rubber surface; idlers support the weight. Understanding how the conveyor actually works — not just what its parts are — is essential to understanding why things go wrong. The entire mechanism depends on three interacting forces: tension, friction, and gravity . MOTOR AC Electric 110–500 kW Coupling GEARBOX Reduces speed Increases torque shaft DRIVE PULLEY → Belt carries coal this way → COAL Idlers (support) TAIL PULLEY ← Return strand (empty belt) ← KEY: Friction at Drive Pulley Pulley surface grips belt → belt moves Tight side tension (High — pulling belt) Slack side tension (Low — returning belt) Take-up (Tension)

children.title: The Three Pillars of Conveyor Motion
children.content: Force / Principle | What It Does | If Disturbed ; Friction (Drive) | The motor turns the drive pulley; the rubber surface of the pulley grips the belt through friction and pulls it forward. Higher friction coating (lagging) on the pulley increases grip. | If coal, water, or grease gets on the pulley surface, friction is lost → belt slips → coal stops moving → pulley overheats. ; Belt Tension | The take-up system maintains a minimum tension in the belt so the belt wraps tightly around the drive pulley. This ensures the friction force can be transmitted effectively. | Too low tension → belt slips on pulley. Too high → bearing overload, structure damage, belt stretch. ; Idler Support | Idlers distribute the weight of the coal-loaded belt across the structure, reducing the effective force the motor must overcome. They also maintain belt shape (troughing). | Failed idler → belt sags → uneven load → increased friction → motor overload → fire risk. The belt tension is not equal everywhere. On the tight side (belt leaving the drive pulley on the carry strand), tension is high — the belt is being pulled. On the slack side (belt returning to the drive pulley), tension is lower. The difference between these two tensions is what propels the belt and coal forward. This concept explains why adequate take-up tension is so critical — insufficient slack-side tension means the drive pulley cannot transmit enough force.

children.title: Why the Belt Drifts (Misalignment)
children.content: The belt naturally tends to drift (wander sideways) if there is any asymmetry — uneven loading, idlers not perfectly perpendicular to belt travel, wind, or a bent frame. Even a slight drift accumulates over the length of the belt. If not corrected, the belt edge contacts the conveyor structure, causing edge damage, spillage, and ultimately belt failure. Self-aligning idlers and training idlers are used to correct drift automatically. A drifted belt that contacts the steel structure can generate enough heat through friction to ignite coal dust — causing a conveyor fire. Belt fires in CHP are a major risk and have caused plant outages lasting weeks.

children.title: Conveyor Capacity & Throughput
children.content: Think of capacity as a "pipe size" — the pipe can carry only so much per second. Push more in than it can carry, and it overflows. Push less, and the plant is underfed. Every belt conveyor is designed to carry a specific maximum tonnage per hour (TPH) . This is called the rated capacity. The conveyor design — belt width, speed, inclination, and idler spacing — is optimised for this rated capacity. Operating at or above this limit causes problems; operating well below causes inefficiency.

children.title: Factors That Determine Capacity
children.content: Factor | How It Affects Capacity | Typical Values (CHP) ; Belt Width | Wider belt = larger cross-sectional area of coal = more tonnes per metre of belt. A wider belt also tolerates larger coal lumps. | 800 mm, 1000 mm, 1200 mm, 1400 mm ; Belt Speed | Higher speed moves the same cross-section faster → more TPH. But higher speed increases dust, wear, and impact at feed points. | 1.2 – 2.5 m/s (typical CHP); up to 4 m/s (high-capacity) ; Trough Angle | Steeper trough (e.g. 35° vs 20°) holds more coal per cross-section. Most CHP conveyors use 35° troughing. | 20°, 25°, 30°, 35°, 45° ; Coal Density & Moisture | Wet coal is heavier per volume → higher tonnage for same volume. However, wet fine coal also sticks to the belt (carryback) and blocks chutes. | Dry coal: ~800 kg/m³; Wet: 900–1000 kg/m³ ; Inclination Angle | Inclined conveyors carry less coal per hour than flat ones at the same belt speed (gravity opposes motion). Steep inclines also risk coal rolling back if belt speed drops. | Max practical: 15°–18° for coal; beyond this, cleated belts needed ; Feed Rate from Feeder | If the upstream feeder delivers more coal than the conveyor is rated for, the belt will be overloaded regardless of its rated capacity. | Controlled via feeder speed (variable frequency drive) When a conveyor is overloaded: (1) coal spills over the belt edges; (2) the motor draws excess current and may trip on overload protection; (3) the belt sags between idlers, increasing friction; (4) the drive may slip; (5) structural stress on the frame increases. Repeated overloading shortens belt life significantly. Underloading (running a conveyor almost empty) wastes electrical energy and accelerates belt wear due to the constant flexing of an unloaded belt over idlers. It also reduces the effective cleaning action of belt cleaners and increases dust generation from the empty belt vibrating on return idlers. A 500 MW thermal unit needs approximately 250–300 TPH of coal at full load. If the belt conveyor can carry 400 TPH rated capacity, there is a buffer. If an upstream crusher or feeder fails and reduces supply to 150 TPH, the bunker level gradually falls and load must be reduced. An intern does not control these rates — but understanding this relationship lets you understand the urgency when a supervisor responds to a falling bunker level.

children.title: Transfer Points & Flow Behaviour
children.content: A transfer point is like a controlled handover baton pass — coal must land precisely on the next belt. Any miss, blockage, or misalignment at this point disrupts the entire downstream flow. Wherever coal moves from one conveyor to the next — or from a hopper to a conveyor — there is a transfer point . These are not minor connections; they are among the most critical and most hazardous locations in the entire Coal Handling Plant. Understanding what happens at a transfer point is essential before entering the CHP. BC-1 (Upper Conveyor) Coal on BC-1 Head Pulley TRANSFER CHUTE (guides coal) ↓ Coal falls here BC-2 (Lower Conveyor) Impact Zone Coal on BC-2 ⚠ DUST ⚠ Spillage ⚠ Spillage ⚠ BLOCKAGE RISK Wet/sticky coal can block chute Coal must land centrally on BC-2 belt. Any deviation → spillage or belt drift.

children.title: What Can Go Wrong at a Transfer Point
children.content: Problem | Cause | Consequence ; Chute Blockage | Wet, fine, or sticky coal accumulates inside the chute and sticks to walls, eventually bridging across. | Coal backs up onto BC-1, causing it to overload. If blockage is not cleared quickly, the conveyor trips. ; Spillage | Coal falls outside the belt edges due to misaligned chute, worn skirt boards, or over-speed discharge. | Accumulation of coal on walkways and structure — slipping hazard, fire risk from dust, structural overloading. ; Dust Generation | Free-fall of coal creates turbulent air that carries fine coal particles. Longer drop height = more dust. | Respiratory hazard, reduced visibility, fire and explosion risk from coal dust cloud. ; Belt Damage at Impact | Large coal lumps falling from height impact the belt at the transfer point, especially if impact idlers are worn. | Belt cover damage, gouging, or even belt puncture — leading to belt failure. ; Off-centre Loading | Coal does not land centrally on BC-2 due to incorrect chute alignment or spillage plate wear. | Belt drifts to one side → edge damage → spillage → potential belt damage against structure. Transfer towers are enclosed structures at junctions between conveyors. They are high-dust, confined-space environments with active machinery on multiple levels. Entry requires a Confined Space Entry Permit, dust mask, and must always be done with a buddy. Never enter during conveyor operation without a specific maintenance permit.

children.title: Safety & Hazard Awareness
children.content: Moving machinery + bulk material + confined spaces = continuous risk. Most conveyor accidents happen not because of complexity but because someone was not aware of where the danger was. You do not need to be doing anything wrong to be injured near a conveyor. You simply need to be in the wrong place, distracted, or unaware of what is moving around you. The conveyor does not slow down for you. It does not have a sensor that detects a human body near it. It will continue running at full speed regardless. Your awareness is your protection. MOVING BELT (entire length is a hazard) TAIL PULLEY 🔴 PINCH ZONE Entanglement risk DRIVE PULLEY 🔴 PINCH + NIP ZONE High-torque crush risk 🟠 FEED POINT Impact hazard Dust cloud 🟠 TRANSFER POINT Spillage, blockage Confined space 🟡 BELT SURFACE Never touch/step on moving belt 🟡 Return strand — carryback coal falls here — slip hazard below ☁ Dust cloud ☁ Dust cloud ━━━ Emergency Pull Cord (full length) — Pull anywhere to STOP conveyor ━━━ HAZARD ZONE LEGEND RED = Extreme danger (pinch/nip/crush) — Mandatory guarding required ORANGE = High hazard (spillage, blockage, dust, confined space) — Permit required YELLOW = Caution zone (moving belt, carryback, slipping) — Stay clear, PPE required

children.title: Hazard-by-Hazard Analysis
children.content: Pulleys rotate continuously at high speed. The nip point — where the belt meets the pulley — has an extremely small gap that closes in milliseconds. A finger, loose clothing, or hair entering this gap will be drawn in with full motor force before any human reaction is possible. Guards (physical covers) must always be in place over all pulleys. If a guard is missing — report it immediately and do not approach the pulley. The belt surface itself is a hazard. Loose clothing, gloves, tools, or anything trailing near the belt can be instantly grabbed and pulled in. Belt speed (1.5–2.5 m/s) is faster than human reflex. This type of accident typically results in degloving injuries, crush injuries, or fatalities. Rule: always wear close-fitting PPE near conveyors. Never lean over a running belt. At transfer points, coal falls from one conveyor to the next. Large coal lumps weighing several kilograms can bounce or be thrown sideways if a blockage or imbalance occurs. Standing below or beside an active chute is extremely dangerous. Transfer towers also have open floors and structural walkways at multiple levels — falling coal from one level can injure personnel on a lower level. Fine coal dust generated at transfer points, feed points, and from carryback is a dual hazard. Respiratory: Coal dust causes coal worker's pneumoconiosis (CWP/"black lung") with long-term exposure. Always wear a P2/P3 dust mask in dusty areas. Fire: Coal dust suspended in air at concentrations above the Lower Explosive Limit (LEL) can ignite from a spark or hot surface. Accumulated coal dust on hot surfaces (like a seized idler or a slipping belt) can also self-ignite. Coal spillage on walkways creates an extremely slippery surface, especially when wet. Carryback coal falls from the return strand onto the floor below the conveyor. Structural platforms, stairs, and walkways in CHP are often narrow and positioned close to moving equipment. Falls from elevated walkways (transfer towers can be 10–20 m high) are fatal. Always hold handrails, wear non-slip safety boots, and never rush on CHP walkways. Conveyor drive panels operate at medium voltage (3.3 kV or 6.6 kV in large plants, 415 V in smaller). Control panels, junction boxes, and local isolators are located along conveyor routes. Never open an electrical panel without a qualified electrician present and without following Lockout-Tagout (LOTO) procedures. Water from coal spillage near electrical panels is extremely dangerous.

children.title: Personal Protective Equipment (PPE) in CHP
children.content: PPE Item | Protection Against | Mandatory In ; Safety Helmet | Falling coal, overhead structures | Entire CHP area ; Safety Boots (steel toe) | Coal impact on foot, slip on spillage | Entire CHP area ; High-Visibility Vest | Visibility to equipment operators | Entire CHP area ; Dust Mask (P2/FFP2 minimum) | Coal dust inhalation | Near transfer points, feed points, tunnels ; Safety Glasses | Coal dust, chipped coal particles | Near active conveyors and transfer points ; Close-fitting Coveralls | Entanglement prevention | Near running conveyors ; Gloves | Coal abrasion, cold metal | During inspection — REMOVE when near rotating parts ; Hearing Protection | Crusher noise (>85 dB) | Near crushers, screeners A red-coloured rope or wire runs the full length of every conveyor, both sides. This is the Emergency Pull Cord (EPC) . Pulling it anywhere along the conveyor immediately stops the conveyor via the Emergency Stop relay. If you see an unsafe condition, an entanglement, or any emergency — pull it. Do not hesitate. A conveyor trip can be restarted after investigation. A human injury cannot be undone. You will never be penalised for pulling the emergency cord in a genuine emergency.

children.title: Types of Wagon Tippler – Upstream Context
children.content: The wagon tippler is the starting gun — the moment coal enters the plant. Different tippler types deliver coal at different rates, lump sizes, and patterns, each with a different impact on the first belt conveyor. Coal arrives at a thermal power plant in railway wagons — each carrying 60–80 tonnes of coal. The wagon tippler is the mechanism that unloads these wagons. The type of tippler directly affects: How quickly coal is unloaded (feed rate) The lump size of coal entering the hopper The loading pattern on the first belt conveyor Dust generation at the unloading point Three Main Types of Wagon Unloading Systems ① Rotary Tippler WAGON HOPPER 150–160° rotation Rotary Tippler Wagon rotated 150–160° on a circular cradle. Wagon stays on rail. Fastest method. Capacity: 1 wagon/12–20 min ⚠ High dust at discharge ② Side Discharge Tippler WAGON HOPPER 45–60° side tilt Side Discharge Tippler Wagon tilts to one side on a pivoted platform. Slower but gentler on the wagon body. Used for bottom-discharge wagons ⚠ Uneven coal distribution ③ Track Hopper System WAGON (No rotation) ↓ Bottom doors ↓ open gravity Grated Track PIT HOPPER Track Hopper System Wagon moves over a grated pit. Bottom-discharge wagons drop coal directly. No tippler. Fastest — continuous unloading ✓ Lowest dust among three types

children.title: Comparison Table
children.content: Feature | Rotary Tippler | Side Discharge Tippler | Track Hopper ; Unloading Method | Rotates wagon 150–160° | Tilts wagon sideways 45–60° | Bottom-discharge through grates ; Wagon Type Required | Any (standard BOX-N wagons) | Side-door wagons | Bottom-discharge BOBR/BOXN-HL wagons ; Unloading Speed | Moderate (12–20 min/wagon) | Slow (20–30 min/wagon) | Fast — continuous ; Coal Lump Size | Can break lumps on impact | Less impact — larger lumps retained | Large lumps pass through grate ; Dust Generation | High (coal falls from height) | Moderate | Low (enclosed pit) ; Feed Consistency | Batch — surge then pause | Batch — gradual | Near-continuous with flow control ; Impact on Conveyor | Surge loading — needs robust feed control | More manageable surges | Steady, easiest on conveyor ; Typical Use in India | Most common (NTPC, APGENCO, etc.) | Older plants | Modern large plants When a rotary tippler unloads a wagon, coal arrives at the hopper in a surge — a large volume in a short time — followed by a pause as the next wagon is positioned. This surge must be absorbed by the hopper before it reaches the feeder and then the belt. If the hopper is small or the feeder is not controlled properly, the surge can overload the belt. Conversely, during the changeover between wagons, the belt may run empty. This cyclic loading is normal for rotary tippler plants, and belt systems are designed to handle it — but a new intern should understand why the loading on the belt appears uneven.

children.title: Critical Process Control Points
children.content: Control points are the locations in the system where the quality, continuity, and safety of coal flow are most sensitive. These are the points a plant engineer monitors most carefully. As an intern, you will hear these terms constantly — understanding what they mean is essential.

children.title: Coal Loading onto Belt (Feed Point)
children.content: Where: Just after the tail pulley, where coal from the hopper/feeder drops onto the moving belt. What is critical here: The coal must be deposited centrally on the belt, at a controlled rate (not exceeding rated TPH), and with minimum free-fall height to reduce impact and dust. Skirt boards must form a tight seal at the edges to contain coal. Any gap in the skirt board → immediate spillage. Overloading at CP-1 causes belt sag, edge spillage, and motor overload. Blocked skirt boards cause belt edge damage. Impact from large coal lumps at feed point damages belt cover.

children.title: Transfer Between Conveyors (Transfer Point)
children.content: Where: Transfer tower — where coal discharges from BC-1 and loads onto BC-2 through a chute. What is critical here: The trajectory of coal through the chute must be matched to the receiving belt speed and direction. The coal must land centrally on BC-2. The chute must be free of blockage. Chute liners (wear-resistant steel plates) must be intact. Deflector plates must direct coal accurately. This is the highest-risk location in the entire CHP. Blockages here can back-fill the chute, causing BC-1 overload. Spillage from here falls from height. Dust is at maximum. Confined space entry here requires a formal permit.

children.title: Belt Movement at Drive Pulley
children.content: Where: Head end of conveyor — drive pulley, motor, gearbox assembly. What is critical here: The drive pulley must maintain sufficient friction with the belt to transmit motor torque without slipping. The belt must wrap around the pulley at the correct arc (wrap angle). The head scraper must effectively remove coal from the belt surface as it discharges. The belt must discharge coal cleanly into the chute below. Extreme mechanical hazard zone. The nip point here has the highest torque in the system. Guard must always be in place. Belt slip here causes overheating and fire. Scraper failure leads to carryback and belt underside fouling.

children.title: Belt Alignment Along Structure
children.content: Where: Monitored continuously along the full length of the conveyor using belt sway switches. What is critical here: The belt must remain centred on the idlers throughout its full length. Belt sway switches are installed at regular intervals — if the belt drifts beyond a set limit, the sway switch first gives an alarm; if drift continues, it trips the conveyor. Self-aligning (training) idlers automatically correct minor drift. Regular inspection of idler alignment and condition is essential to maintaining belt tracking. Belt drift → edge contact with structure → friction heat → fire risk. Spillage along the full belt length. Edge damage requires expensive belt replacement.

children.title: Discharge at Coal Bunker
children.content: Where: Head end of the final conveyor — above the coal bunker. What is critical here: Coal must discharge into the correct bunker bay. In large plants, a tripper car (a movable discharge device on the belt) distributes coal across multiple bunker bays to maintain even filling. Bunker level indicators monitor how full each bay is. If a bunker overflows, coal falls into the boiler bay — a serious fire and housekeeping hazard. If a bunker starves, the boiler load must be reduced immediately. Bunker overflow → coal on boiler bay floor → fire risk near hot surfaces. Bunker starvation → forced load reduction → revenue loss. Dust in bunker bay is particularly hazardous — bunker bays are semi-enclosed high-dust zones.

children.title: Consequences When the System Fails
children.content: Understanding failure consequences is not pessimism — it is the foundation of safety and operational discipline. Every component has a reason it exists, and that reason becomes clear the moment it fails. Below is a structured view of what happens when the belt conveyor system fails, across three dimensions.

children.title: 🏭 Plant Continuity
children.content: Conveyor stoppage → coal supply interrupted → bunker level falls within hours Bunker starvation → boiler load must be reduced → generation loss (MW reduction) Prolonged stoppage → boiler trips → complete unit shutdown Flow imbalance (feeder too fast) → belt overload → conveyor trips → same outcome Downstream impact on grid: power deficit, frequency instability Estimated loss per hour of outage for a 500 MW unit: ₹15–25 lakhs (at current rates)

children.title: ⚙ Machinery Integrity
children.content: Belt damage from overload or misalignment → longitudinal rip → belt replacement (₹5–50 lakhs per belt) Idler seizure → local friction → belt fire → possible total belt loss Drive pulley slip → overheating of lagging → rubber deterioration → reduced friction → more slip Gearbox overload from blocked conveyor → gear damage → weeks of downtime Take-up failure → belt slack → catastrophic slippage and pile-up at head end Transfer chute wear → liner failure → chute structural damage → extended shutdown

children.title: 👷 Human Safety
children.content: Entanglement in moving belt → degloving, amputation, fatality Entanglement in drive pulley nip → instant, irreversible crush injury Falling coal at transfer point → blunt trauma, fracture Belt fire → smoke inhalation, burn injuries Coal dust explosion → blast and burn injuries across large area Slipping on coal spillage → fall from height in transfer towers (potentially fatal) Electrical contact near damaged panels → electrocution Every failure in this list was, at some point, preventable . Most machinery failures begin with a small defect — a seized idler, a worn scraper, a loose guard, a misaligned belt — that was visible for days before the failure happened. The difference between a major accident and a near-miss is often one person who was paying attention and reported what they saw. As an intern, your most valuable contribution to plant safety is having the awareness to recognise and report early signs of deterioration — and this course is giving you exactly that awareness.

children.title: Real Failure Scenarios – Cause & Effect Analysis
children.content: The following failure scenarios are based on common real-world incidents in Coal Handling Plants across India and globally. Study each one carefully — during your site visit, you should be able to recognise the early warning signs of each.

children.title: Uneven Loading → Belt Drift → Structural Damage
children.content: Cause: Coal from the feeder drops consistently to one side of the belt (e.g., feeder gate partially blocked, chute misaligned). The belt carries more load on one side than the other. What Happens: The belt gradually drifts toward the heavier side. It contacts the steel frame of the conveyor structure. Friction between the belt edge and the frame generates heat. Over hours, the belt edge begins to abrade. Coal spillage begins at the affected side. If not corrected, the belt tears longitudinally — a full-length split requiring complete belt replacement. Early Signs: Belt sway alarm activates. Visible drift at one or more idler sets. Spillage on one side only. Squealing noise from belt-structure contact. Consequence: Forced conveyor shutdown. Belt replacement cost (₹10–40 lakhs). 2–5 days of downtime for re-belting.
children.parent_title: Real Failure Scenarios – Cause & Effect Analysis

children.title: Overloading → Belt Stress → Spillage → Motor Trip
children.content: Cause: The feeder speed is set too high, or a sudden surge from the wagon tippler overwhelms the hopper. Coal falls on the belt at a rate exceeding rated capacity. What Happens: Coal piles up on the belt, exceeding the trough capacity. Spillage occurs from both edges. The belt sags more between idlers, increasing rolling resistance. Motor current rises. Motor protection relay detects overload and trips the motor. The belt stops. Coal continues to fall from the hopper onto the stationary belt, burying it under a pile of coal. Early Signs: High motor current alarm. Increased spillage at feed point. Belt visibly overloaded (coal reaching edge of trough). Vibration increase. Consequence: Conveyor buried under coal. Manual digging-out required (hours of labour). Belt may be damaged under the weight. Entire coal flow stopped.
children.parent_title: Real Failure Scenarios – Cause & Effect Analysis

children.title: Poor Transfer Point Flow → Chute Blockage → System Shutdown
children.content: Cause: Wet, fine coal (after rain or due to high moisture content) builds up on the inner walls of the transfer chute. Over time, coal bridges across the chute opening. What Happens: Coal flow through the chute reduces, then stops. BC-1 continues running — coal piles up at the head pulley discharge point and overflows the chute. BC-2 runs empty, drawing coal from the bunker without being replenished. Bunker level falls. Eventually, BC-1 is tripped on overload as coal piles up. The plant is called to reduce load. Early Signs: BC-2 belt running empty (visible drop in load current). Spillage at base of transfer chute. Unusual noise from chute (hollow sound instead of coal flow sound). Consequence: Manual chute cleaning required. Confined space permit needed. Risk of coal avalanche when blockage suddenly clears.
children.parent_title: Real Failure Scenarios – Cause & Effect Analysis

children.title: Belt Slipping on Drive Pulley → Loss of Conveying → Overheating
children.content: Cause: Water or coal slurry contaminates the surface of the drive pulley, reducing friction. Or the take-up tension is insufficient. The belt cannot maintain grip on the rotating pulley. What Happens: The drive pulley continues to rotate, but the belt slips — moving slower than the pulley surface. This generates significant heat at the pulley-belt contact zone. The rubber lagging on the pulley begins to burn. Acrid smoke is generated. If the conveyor is not stopped, the lagging is destroyed, and eventually the belt itself can ignite. Meanwhile, coal stops moving because the belt is stationary or barely moving. Early Signs: Burning rubber smell. Smoke from head end. Reduced belt speed indicator. High motor current (motor is working hard but belt is not moving at designed speed). Consequence: Belt fire — major safety incident. Drive pulley lagging replacement. Potential partial belt damage. 1–3 days outage.
children.parent_title: Real Failure Scenarios – Cause & Effect Analysis

children.title: Dust Accumulation Ignition → Conveyor Fire
children.content: Cause: Coal dust accumulates on conveyor structure, idlers, and the underside of the belt over weeks without adequate housekeeping. A seized idler generates frictional heat. This heat ignites the accumulated coal dust. What Happens: Smouldering begins on the structure or inside the belt tunnel. Because coal dust is distributed over a large area, the fire can spread rapidly along the full length of the conveyor. In an enclosed conveyor (gallery), fire and smoke can develop quickly. A conveyor fire can destroy the entire belt (hundreds of metres long), the structure, and adjacent equipment. Early Signs: Burning smell. Smoke in the conveyor gallery. Seized idler (idler not rotating despite belt moving — creates a flat worn spot on the idler and local heating). Unusual hotspot detected by thermal camera. Consequence: Major fire incident. Full belt replacement. Structural repairs. Plant outage of weeks. Regulatory investigation. Possible fatalities if personnel are in the gallery.
children.parent_title: Real Failure Scenarios – Cause & Effect Analysis

children.title: Exposure to Moving Parts → Entanglement Injury
children.content: Cause: A person reaches over or near a running conveyor without adequate clearance. Loose clothing, gloves, or hair contacts the moving belt or a rotating idler/pulley. What Happens: The belt instantly grips the material and draws the person's limb or clothing into the nip point. At 1.5 m/s belt speed and with a motor delivering hundreds of kilowatts, the force is thousands of times greater than human strength. No one can pull free. The injury is instantaneous and typically irreversible — degloving, crush, amputation, or fatal entrapment. Prevention: Guard all nip points (mandatory, not optional). Never approach a running conveyor without proper authorisation. Emergency pull cord must be functional and tested. Buddy system — never work alone near running equipment. Consequence: Serious injury or fatality. Plant shutdown for investigation. Management liability. Irreparable human loss. There is zero tolerance in a professional plant for bypassing guards, reaching over running conveyors, or working near running equipment without proper PPE and procedures. This is not bureaucracy — it is the direct lesson from real fatalities.
children.parent_title: Real Failure Scenarios – Cause & Effect Analysis

children.title: You Are L1-Ready When You Can…
children.content: A trainee is considered ready for site induction (L1 complete) when they can demonstrate the following outcomes — not just recall them, but explain them in their own words to a senior engineer: End-to-End Coal Flow: Clearly explain how coal travels from the railway wagon through the wagon tippler, hopper, feeder, conveyors, transfer points, and finally into the bunker and boiler — and what each stage depends on. Component Identification: Walk along a conveyor and correctly name and describe the function of the belt, drive pulley, tail pulley, idlers, take-up system, scrapers, feed point, and all guards and safety devices. Mechanism Understanding: Explain how motion is generated (motor → gearbox → drive pulley → friction → belt), why tension is critical, how idlers support the belt, and why belt drift occurs and is dangerous. Capacity Awareness: Explain the factors that affect conveyor capacity (belt width, speed, inclination, coal density), what overloading and underloading look like, and why both are problematic for the plant. Hazard Identification: Point to and describe every high-risk zone on a conveyor (pinch points, moving belt, transfer points, dust zones), explain the associated injury types, and correctly identify the emergency pull cord and its purpose. Failure Consequence Awareness: Describe at least 4 failure scenarios, their early warning signs, and their consequences for plant continuity, machinery integrity, and human safety — without reading from notes.

children.title: Instrumentation & Safety Devices on the Conveyor
children.content: Think of instrumentation as the conveyor's nervous system — sensors spread across the full length that continuously sense abnormal conditions and either warn operators or automatically stop the machine before a small problem becomes a catastrophe. A belt conveyor in a modern Coal Handling Plant is fitted with numerous sensors, switches, and protective devices along its entire length. These are not optional extras — they are mandatory safety and operational requirements under Indian Electricity Rules, factory safety regulations, and plant operating procedures. As an intern, you will see these devices everywhere on the conveyor. Knowing what each one does is essential. MOVING BELT TAIL PULLEY DRIVE PULLEY M ━━ EMERGENCY PULL CORD (Both Sides, Full Length) ━━ EPC EPC EPC BSW Belt Sway Switch BSW ZSS SPD Zero Speed / Underspeed Switch BW WEIGH Belt Weigher (Load cell) CBD CHUTE Chute Blocked Detector 🔥 Thermal/ Fire Detector Return Strand EPC = Emergency Pull Cord BSW = Belt Sway Switch ZSS = Zero Speed Switch BW = Belt Weigher CBD = Chute Blocked Detector 🔥 = Fire Detector

children.title: Safety Device Reference Guide
children.content: Device | Location on Conveyor | Function | Response When Activated ; Emergency Pull Cord (EPC) | Both sides, full length of conveyor, approximately every 30–50 m | Allows any person anywhere along the conveyor to immediately stop it in an emergency by pulling the rope/wire | Immediate emergency stop of conveyor drive motor. Conveyor cannot restart until EPC is reset and root cause investigated. ; Belt Sway Switch (BSW) | Both sides, spaced every 50–75 m along carry and return strand | Detects lateral drift of the belt beyond a set limit. Has two positions: first position = alarm; second position = trip. | First activation: Alarm in control room. Second (greater drift): Conveyor trip. Prevents belt edge from contacting steel structure. ; Zero Speed Switch (ZSS) | Tail pulley shaft or on a return idler | Monitors belt speed. Detects if the belt has stopped (zero speed) while the motor is still running — indicating belt slip. | Conveyor trip + alarm. Prevents drive pulley from running against a stationary belt (which causes fire from friction). ; Belt Weigher (BW) | Fixed location on the conveyor, typically mid-span | Measures the weight of coal on the belt per unit length using load cells. Calculates instantaneous TPH and cumulative tonnes. | Data sent to control room / DCS. No trip — provides operational data. High load may trigger an alarm. ; Chute Blocked Detector (CBD) | Inside transfer chutes at transfer points | Detects when coal has accumulated and blocked the chute (using vibration probe, ultrasonic, or paddle switch). | Alarm in control room. May automatically stop upstream feeder to prevent further coal accumulation. ; Thermal / Fire Detector | Inside conveyor galleries (tunnels) and transfer towers | Detects elevated temperature indicating a developing fire. Linear heat detection cable runs along the belt gallery roof. | Fire alarm. Conveyor trip. Activation of fire suppression system (CO₂ or water mist). Control room alert. ; Underspeed Switch | Drive shaft area | Detects if belt is running slower than designed speed (but not zero). Indicates overloading or drive slip developing. | Alarm → trip if underspeed persists. Allows early intervention before full slippage occurs. ; Motor Overload Relay (OLR) | Motor control centre (MCC) / switchgear panel | Monitors motor current. If the motor draws current above the rated limit for a set time (indicating overload), it trips. | Motor trip + alarm. Conveyor stops. Investigation required to identify overload cause before restart. When you walk a conveyor on site, you will see red ropes, yellow boxes, and small switches mounted on the frame at regular intervals — these are all part of this safety system. You will hear terms like "BSW trip," "ZSS alarm," or "EPC activation" on the radio constantly. Now you know exactly what each term means, what triggered it, and what the plant team needs to do in response. On some plants, under production pressure, well-meaning but incorrect actions include bypassing a belt sway switch that keeps tripping, disabling a chute blocked detector that gives "false" alarms, or tying off an EPC that was accidentally pulled. This is an extremely dangerous practice. Every safety device bypass removes one layer of protection from the system. Multiple bypasses create a condition where a fatal accident can occur without any warning. As an intern, if you are ever asked to bypass a safety device, immediately consult your supervisor. Document it. Never accept it as routine.

children.title: Your First Site Visit – What to Observe & What to Look For
children.content: Your first site visit is not a tour — it is a structured observation exercise. For every component you studied in this course, there is a physical object in front of you. Treat it like matching a textbook diagram to a real machine, component by component. Now that you understand the system theoretically, you need to translate that knowledge to what you will actually see, hear, and smell when you walk into the Coal Handling Plant for the first time. This guide prepares you for that transition, so you do not feel overwhelmed or miss important details. Site Visit Observation Sequence – Walk the Conveyor Like an Engineer STEP 1 Start at the Feed Point (Tail End) Observe loading STEP 2 Walk Along One Side of Belt Check belt & idlers STEP 3 Observe Drive / Head End Check discharge STEP 4 Look at Safety Devices EPC, sway switches STEP 5 Visit Transfer Tower (outside) Observe from safe zone STEP 6 – REFLECT & REPORT Note all abnormalities observed. Discuss with supervisor. NEVER act on abnormalities independently. ⛔ NEVER do this on your first visit: Do not touch, adjust, or interfere with any equipment — observe only.

children.title: Step-by-Step: What to Look For at Each Location
children.content: Location | What a Healthy System Looks Like | Warning Signs to Report ; Feed Point (Tail End) | Coal lands centrally on the belt. Skirt boards are close to the belt surface with no visible gap. No coal spillage outside the belt edges. Dust suppression sprays (if fitted) are operating. | Coal spilling over belt edges. Gap between skirt board and belt. Coal piling up at sides. Dust cloud larger than usual. Unusual impact noise from large lumps. ; Belt Surface (While Walking Alongside) | Belt is centred on idlers. Surface is intact — no cuts, gouges, or longitudinal slits. Coal is uniformly distributed across the belt width. Belt moves smoothly without lateral wandering. | Belt visibly off-centre (drift). Belt edge near or touching structure. Cuts or rips on belt surface. Uneven coal load (all on one side). Belt flapping or vibrating excessively. ; Idlers (Along the Full Length) | All idlers are spinning freely as the belt passes over them. No noise from any individual idler. No flat spot on any roller (from seizure). All idlers are in their correct mounting position. | Any idler NOT spinning (seized — belt slides over it creating heat). Grinding or squealing noise from an idler bearing. Idler shell worn flat on one spot. Idler hanging loose or displaced from its bracket. ; Structure & Walkway (Below the Belt) | Walkway is clean — minimal coal spillage on the floor. Structure is intact. No coal accumulated on structural members. Return strand is clean (minimal carryback coal on the underside). | Coal accumulated on structural members (fire risk). Excessive carryback falling onto the floor below. Wet coal mix on walkway (slip hazard). Smell of burning rubber or coal smoke. ; Drive / Head End | Coal discharges cleanly over the head pulley into the chute. Belt scraper is in contact with the belt and removing carryback. Head pulley guard is in place. No burning smell. Motor noise is normal (steady hum). | Coal not discharging cleanly (flying off sideways). Burning rubber smell (belt slipping on pulley). Unusual motor noise (overload — grinding or laboured hum). Scraper not in contact with belt. Any guard missing. ; Safety Devices | All EPC ropes are present, unbroken, and at the correct tension (not sagging to ground, not over-tight). Belt sway switches are mounted and free. No safety device is taped up, bypassed, or disabled. | EPC rope broken, missing, or sagging. Sway switch blocked with coal or debris. Any safety device with a bypass tag or wire tied in bypassed position. Missing nip point guards at pulleys. ; Transfer Tower (from outside / entrance) | Coal flow sound is continuous and steady from inside (not intermittent). No coal spillage on the outside of the tower base. Dust seal curtains at openings are intact. | Silence from chute (blockage). Coal spilling from tower base. Dust escaping from every gap (excess spillage inside). Unusual vibration of the tower structure. As an intern, you will not be allowed to operate equipment. But you can walk the conveyors during your inspection rounds with a supervisor, and you can see things that busy operators may have overlooked . A fresh pair of eyes — trained by this course to know what is normal and what is not — can catch an early warning sign that prevents a major failure. Always report what you observe to your supervisor, and never assume "someone else must have seen it already."

children.title: Do's and Don'ts for the Intern in the Coal Handling Plant
children.content: This section translates your theoretical learning into specific behaviours. These are not rules imposed on you — they are the behaviours that keep you alive and healthy during your internship and throughout your career in the power industry.

children.title: ✅ DO – Always
children.content: ✔ Always wear your complete PPE before entering the CHP area — helmet, boots, high-vis vest, and dust mask at minimum. ✔ Always stay on designated walkways. Never take shortcuts across structural members or below return strands. ✔ Always walk in pairs (buddy system) inside CHP, especially in galleries and near transfer towers. ✔ Always report abnormalities (seized idler, missing guard, damaged EPC) to your supervisor immediately — verbally and in writing. ✔ Always ask for a proper explanation before approaching any equipment you have not previously been briefed on. ✔ Always maintain a minimum clearance of 1 metre from the belt and moving machinery unless you are following a supervised inspection protocol. ✔ Always wear close-fitting clothing. Tuck in shirts. No loose ties, scarves, or dangling lanyards. ✔ Always know the location of the nearest Emergency Pull Cord and fire extinguisher on any conveyor you are walking. ✔ Always pull the EPC without hesitation if you see an entanglement, smoke, or fire — never wait for confirmation.
children.parent_title: Do's and Don'ts for the Intern in the Coal Handling Plant

children.title: ⛔ DON'T – Never
children.content: ✘ Never touch a moving belt — not to feel the speed, test the surface, or remove a piece of coal from it. ✘ Never lean over a running conveyor for any reason — not to look at the other side, not to pick up a fallen object. ✘ Never attempt to clear a blocked chute or dislodged coal from a running conveyor using your hands, feet, or tools. ✘ Never remove guards from pulleys or other rotating parts — even "just to check" something. ✘ Never silence or bypass a safety alarm without a supervisor's explicit authorisation and a proper investigation. ✘ Never enter a transfer tower, conveyor gallery, or any confined space without a valid Confined Space Entry Permit. ✘ Never operate any switch, valve, or control on the conveyor unless specifically instructed and supervised by an authorised engineer. ✘ Never work alone in the CHP — especially in conveyor galleries, transfer towers, and tunnels below trestle conveyors. ✘ Never assume a stopped conveyor is safe without confirming it is Locked Out / Tagged Out (LOTO) by a qualified person. One of the most common causes of serious injury in industrial plants is working on equipment that appears to be stopped but is not properly isolated. A conveyor belt that stopped due to an alarm can be restarted from the control room while someone is working on it. The Lockout-Tagout (LOTO) procedure requires the drive to be electrically isolated at the switchgear, locked with a physical padlock, and tagged with the worker's identity before any maintenance work begins. As an intern, you must never approach any equipment for maintenance purposes. If asked to, immediately request that proper LOTO isolation is carried out and confirmed before you go near the equipment.

children.title: Glossary of CHP & Belt Conveyor Terms
children.content: On your first day on site you will hear these terms constantly. This glossary ensures you are not lost in the conversation. Term | Meaning ; Belt | The continuous rubber-fabric loop that carries coal from tail to head end. ; Belt Conveyor (BC) | The complete conveyor assembly — numbered in sequence (BC-1, BC-2, etc.) in the plant. ; Carry Strand | The top run of the belt that carries coal toward the discharge point. ; Return Strand | The lower run of the empty belt going back from head to tail. ; Head Pulley | The drive pulley at the discharge end of the conveyor. ; Tail Pulley | The non-driven pulley at the loading end. ; Idler | A free-spinning roller that supports the belt. Troughing idlers (carry) and flat idlers (return). ; Trough Angle | The angle at which wing idler rolls are tilted to form the trough (20°–45°). ; Take-up | The tensioning device — gravity, screw, or hydraulic — that keeps the belt at correct tension. ; Lagging | Rubber coating on the drive pulley surface to increase friction with the belt. ; Skirt Board | Side rubber/steel walls at the feed point that contain coal on the belt edge. ; Scraper / Cleaner | A blade pressed against the belt at the head end to remove carryback coal. ; Carryback | Fine coal that sticks to the belt after discharge and is carried back on the return strand. ; Transfer Point | Location where coal moves from one conveyor to the next via a chute. ; Chute | The steel guide structure that directs coal from one conveyor to the next at transfer points. ; Tripper Car | A movable discharge device on a conveyor above the bunker that distributes coal across bunker bays. Term | Meaning ; Bunker | Large coal storage silo above the boiler, fed by the conveyor. Buffer for continuous boiler feeding. ; Hopper | A funnel-shaped collection vessel below the wagon tippler that collects unloaded coal. ; Feeder | A device (vibrating, apron, or belt type) that controls the rate of coal feeding onto the conveyor. ; TPH | Tonnes Per Hour — the standard unit of conveyor throughput capacity. ; CHP | Coal Handling Plant — the entire system for receiving, processing, and conveying coal in a power plant. ; DCS | Distributed Control System — the central computerised control system monitoring all CHP parameters. ; MCC | Motor Control Centre — the electrical switchgear panel that starts, stops, and protects conveyor motors. ; EPC | Emergency Pull Cord — the safety rope running the full length of the conveyor for emergency stop. ; BSW | Belt Sway Switch — sensor that detects lateral belt drift and triggers alarm/trip. ; ZSS / USS | Zero Speed Switch / Underspeed Switch — detects belt slippage or stall. ; LOTO | Lockout-Tagout — energy isolation procedure before maintenance on conveyor or any equipment. ; Nip Point | The point where the belt meets a pulley — the most dangerous entanglement zone. ; Belt Drift | Lateral wandering of the belt off centre — can cause edge damage and fire. ; Tight Side | The belt strand leaving the drive pulley (carry side) — where belt tension is highest. ; Slack Side | The belt strand returning to the drive pulley — where tension is lower. ; CWP | Coal Workers' Pneumoconiosis — lung disease caused by long-term coal dust inhalation ("black lung").

text_chunks.title: How to Use This Course
text_chunks.content: How to Use This Course This course is designed to build your mental picture of the Coal Handling Plant's belt conveyor system before you set foot on the physical site. Think of it as downloading the entire system into your mind so that when you arrive, you recognise what you see, understand why it exists, and know where the dangers are. This is a context and awareness course only. It does not teach you how to start, stop, or operate any equipment. You must never attempt any operational action independently without formal training and authorisation from the plant management. After completing this course you will be able to walk around a Coal Handling Plant, identify every major component of the belt conveyor system, understand its role in power generation, and — most importantly — recognise hazardous zones and behaviours that could injure you or others.

text_chunks.title: Purpose of the Belt Conveyor System
text_chunks.content: Purpose of the Belt Conveyor System The belt conveyor is the continuous coal transport pipeline inside the plant — like the bloodstream of the power plant. A thermal power plant burns coal to generate steam, which drives a turbine, which spins a generator to produce electricity. The entire generation cycle depends on one simple but critical requirement: a continuous, uninterrupted supply of coal to the boiler . That is exactly what the belt conveyor system does. It is the internal transportation network that moves coal — hundreds or thousands of tonnes per day — from the point where it is received (the wagon tippler / track hopper) to the coal bunkers located above the boilers. From the bunkers, coal flows down to the pulverisers (mills) that grind it into powder for combustion. Coal Mine / Railway Wagon BELT CONVEYOR SYSTEM (CHP) ← This Course → Coal Bunker & Pulveriser Boiler (Combustion) Turbine & Generator Coal-to-electricity conversion chain — Belt Conveyor is Stage 2 If the belt conveyor stops for any reason — mechanical failure, blockage, power trip, misalignment — coal stops moving. Within minutes, the bunker level drops. Within hours, boiler load has to be reduced. If not restored quickly, the entire generating unit may shut down, causing a loss of hundreds of megawatts from the grid. That is the direct consequence of this system failing. In a typical 500 MW coal-fired unit, the conveyor system must deliver approximately 250–300 tonnes of coal per hour continuously. Any interruption has an immediate, measurable cost — both financial and to the reliability of the power supply.

text_chunks.title: System Flow Integration – End-to-End View
text_chunks.content: System Flow Integration – End-to-End View Wagon Tippler → Hopper → Feeder → Conveyor → Transfer Points → Coal Bunker → Boiler. The conveyor is not isolated — it is one link in a synchronised chain. Before you can understand the conveyor itself, you need to visualise the complete material flow — the journey coal takes from the moment it arrives at the plant to when it reaches the boiler. Think of it like a factory assembly line: every station depends on the one before it, and supplies the one after it. RAILWAY WAGON (Coal Source) Arrival point WAGON TIPPLER (Unloading) ~20–25 min/wagon TRACK HOPPER (Buffer) Coal storage pit FEEDER / CRUSHER (Sizing) Controls feed rate BELT CONVEYOR BC-1 (This Course) Primary conveying TRANSFER TOWER (High-risk zone) BC-1 → BC-2 COAL BUNKER (Final Buffer) Above the boiler BOILER (Combustion) ⚠ CRITICAL DELIVERY ZONE Transfer Tower + Bunker filling = high-risk area Coal Flow Direction → Each station is dependent on the previous — disruption at any point affects the entire chain

text_chunks.title: Understanding Each Stage
text_chunks.content: Understanding Each Stage Stage | What Happens Here | Consequence if Disrupted ; Railway Wagon | Coal-loaded wagons arrive from the mine via rail. Each wagon carries 60–80 tonnes. | No coal input — entire downstream system starves. ; Wagon Tippler / Track Hopper | Wagon is inverted or coal falls through a grated pit. Coal drops into the hopper below. | Feed is interrupted — hopper level drops, feeder starves. ; Track Hopper / Surge Hopper | Acts as a buffer storage. Absorbs variation in wagon unloading rate. Feeds the conveyor steadily. | Overflow if feed is too fast; starvation if empty. ; Feeder / Crusher | Controls the rate at which coal is loaded onto the conveyor. May include a crusher to reduce lump size. | Overload or underload on conveyor; blockages if lumps are too large. ; Belt Conveyor BC-1 | Carries coal horizontally or at an incline to the transfer tower or directly to the bunker. | Entire downstream coal supply stops. ; Transfer Tower | Junction point where coal moves from one conveyor to another (BC-1 to BC-2). Contains a chute to guide coal. | Spillage, blockage, or coal misdirection. ; Coal Bunker | Large overhead storage silo (capacity 8–12 hours of operation). Continuously fed from conveyor above. | Bunker starves → boiler load reduction → unit outage. ; Boiler | Coal from bunker is pulverised and fired. Steam drives the turbine-generator. | Power generation stops. The belt conveyor is not an isolated machine . It is one critical link in a chain. An imbalance at any point — too much coal, too little coal, wrong size coal — travels downstream and amplifies. A senior engineer thinks of the entire chain simultaneously, not just the conveyor belt in front of them.

text_chunks.title: Conveyor Components & Layout
text_chunks.content: Conveyor Components & Layout A moving belt supported and driven across a structured path — like a moving staircase carrying coal instead of people. Before you can work safely near a belt conveyor, you must be able to name every component, point to it, and describe its function . On a real plant, supervisors will test this knowledge before allowing you near the equipment. Below is a systematic walkthrough of every major component. TAIL Tail Pulley DRIVE PULLEY Head/Drive Pulley CARRYING STRAND (Coal on top) Return Strand (empty belt going back) COAL LOAD Carry Idlers Return Idler Take-up (Tension) MOTOR + GEARBOX ↓ Feed Point (From Hopper) → Belt Travel Direction → Scraper Belt Cross-Section (Troughed Configuration) Centre Roll Wing Roll Wing Roll COAL ← Belt (Troughed) → Trough angle: typically 20°–35° Troughing increases carrying capacity vs flat belt 20–35°
breadcrumb: Belt Conveyor Operation – L1 Foundational Course | CHP Training

text_chunks.title: 🔴 Belt
text_chunks.content: 🔴 Belt The belt is the actual carrying medium — the surface on which coal rests and moves. It is made of multiple layers: rubber covers on top and bottom, with reinforcing fabric plies (nylon, polyester, or steel cords) in between. The belt forms a continuous loop — the top strand carries coal forward; the bottom (return) strand travels empty back to the start. A typical CHP belt is 800–1400 mm wide and can be hundreds of metres long. The belt edge is sharp when damaged. The belt surface can drag anything that contacts it. Never stand on or reach over a moving belt.
breadcrumb: Belt Conveyor Operation – L1 Foundational Course | CHP Training

text_chunks.title: 🔵 Drive Unit (Motor + Gearbox + Drive Pulley)
text_chunks.content: 🔵 Drive Unit (Motor + Gearbox + Drive Pulley) This is the power source of the conveyor. An electric motor (typically 110–500 kW in a CHP) drives a gearbox that reduces speed and increases torque. The gearbox output shaft is connected to the drive pulley (also called the head pulley). The belt wraps around this pulley, and friction between the pulley surface and the belt drives the entire system. The drive pulley is always at the discharge (head) end. Pinch point between belt and drive pulley. Extremely high force — instantly fatal if contacted. Must always have a fixed guard.
breadcrumb: Belt Conveyor Operation – L1 Foundational Course | CHP Training

text_chunks.title: 🟡 Idlers
text_chunks.content: 🟡 Idlers Idlers are the support rollers that keep the belt in shape and prevent it from sagging under the weight of coal. They are spaced every 1–1.5 metres along the top (carry) strand. Carry idlers are usually mounted in a 3-roll troughing configuration to form a trough shape. Return idlers support the empty belt on the return path and are usually flat or slightly tilted. Idlers rotate freely, reducing friction on the belt. Failed (seized) idlers can cause friction, heat, and fire. They also cause belt misalignment. A spinning idler can trap cloth or fingers.
breadcrumb: Belt Conveyor Operation – L1 Foundational Course | CHP Training

text_chunks.title: ⚪ Tail Pulley
text_chunks.content: ⚪ Tail Pulley Located at the loading (start) end of the conveyor. The tail pulley is a plain pulley — it does not drive the belt. Its role is simply to act as the return point where the belt loops back. The feed point (where coal drops from the hopper/feeder) is usually just after the tail pulley. The tail pulley is also where belt tension is lowest, making slippage in this region less dangerous — but still a pinch hazard.
breadcrumb: Belt Conveyor Operation – L1 Foundational Course | CHP Training

text_chunks.title: 🟣 Take-up System
text_chunks.content: 🟣 Take-up System The belt, like any loop under load, must be kept at the correct tension — not too tight, not too loose. If tension is too low, the belt slips on the drive pulley. If too high, bearings and structure are overloaded. The take-up system maintains this tension automatically. In a gravity take-up , a weighted carriage pulls the tail pulley backward using gravity. In a screw take-up , the tail pulley position is adjusted manually. In heavy-duty conveyors, an automatic hydraulic or winch-type take-up is used.
breadcrumb: Belt Conveyor Operation – L1 Foundational Course | CHP Training

text_chunks.title: 🟤 Feed Point (Loading Zone)
text_chunks.content: 🟤 Feed Point (Loading Zone) This is where coal is loaded from the hopper or feeder onto the belt. The feed point includes impact idlers (heavier-duty rollers to absorb the impact of falling coal) and skirt boards (rubber or steel side walls that contain the coal on the belt as it is loaded and prevent spillage at the edges). The alignment and height of the drop point critically affects belt loading quality. Spillage is highest at feed points. Wet or fine coal can also block the skirt boards, causing pressure on the belt edge.
breadcrumb: Belt Conveyor Operation – L1 Foundational Course | CHP Training

text_chunks.title: 🟠 Scrapers & Belt Cleaners
text_chunks.content: 🟠 Scrapers & Belt Cleaners After coal is discharged at the head pulley, a thin layer of fine coal adheres to the belt surface and carries back on the return strand. This is called carryback . Scrapers are blades pressed against the belt surface (at the head pulley and along the return path) to remove this carryback. Without effective scrapers, carryback falls off along the return path, causing spillage, dust, and idler fouling everywhere under the belt.
breadcrumb: Belt Conveyor Operation – L1 Foundational Course | CHP Training

text_chunks.title: 🔷 Structure, Walkways & Guards
text_chunks.content: 🔷 Structure, Walkways & Guards The conveyor is mounted on a steel frame (truss or box structure) that keeps everything aligned and at the correct height. Walkways run alongside for inspection. Nip guards are fitted at all pulley-belt contact points. Emergency pull cords (emergency stop cables) run the full length of the conveyor — pulling the cord anywhere on the conveyor stops it immediately. These are life-saving devices and must never be bypassed. If you see a guard removed or a pull cord damaged, report it immediately. These are mandatory safety devices.
breadcrumb: Belt Conveyor Operation – L1 Foundational Course | CHP Training

text_chunks.title: Functional Mechanism of Conveying
text_chunks.content: Functional Mechanism of Conveying Friction-driven continuous loop — the motor grips the belt through the drive pulley; the belt carries coal through friction between coal and rubber surface; idlers support the weight. Understanding how the conveyor actually works — not just what its parts are — is essential to understanding why things go wrong. The entire mechanism depends on three interacting forces: tension, friction, and gravity . MOTOR AC Electric 110–500 kW Coupling GEARBOX Reduces speed Increases torque shaft DRIVE PULLEY → Belt carries coal this way → COAL Idlers (support) TAIL PULLEY ← Return strand (empty belt) ← KEY: Friction at Drive Pulley Pulley surface grips belt → belt moves Tight side tension (High — pulling belt) Slack side tension (Low — returning belt) Take-up (Tension)
breadcrumb: Belt Conveyor Operation – L1 Foundational Course | CHP Training
child_titles: The Three Pillars of Conveyor Motion

text_chunks.title: The Three Pillars of Conveyor Motion
text_chunks.content: The Three Pillars of Conveyor Motion Force / Principle | What It Does | If Disturbed ; Friction (Drive) | The motor turns the drive pulley; the rubber surface of the pulley grips the belt through friction and pulls it forward. Higher friction coating (lagging) on the pulley increases grip. | If coal, water, or grease gets on the pulley surface, friction is lost → belt slips → coal stops moving → pulley overheats. ; Belt Tension | The take-up system maintains a minimum tension in the belt so the belt wraps tightly around the drive pulley. This ensures the friction force can be transmitted effectively. | Too low tension → belt slips on pulley. Too high → bearing overload, structure damage, belt stretch. ; Idler Support | Idlers distribute the weight of the coal-loaded belt across the structure, reducing the effective force the motor must overcome. They also maintain belt shape (troughing). | Failed idler → belt sags → uneven load → increased friction → motor overload → fire risk. The belt tension is not equal everywhere. On the tight side (belt leaving the drive pulley on the carry strand), tension is high — the belt is being pulled. On the slack side (belt returning to the drive pulley), tension is lower. The difference between these two tensions is what propels the belt and coal forward. This concept explains why adequate take-up tension is so critical — insufficient slack-side tension means the drive pulley cannot transmit enough force.
breadcrumb: Belt Conveyor Operation – L1 Foundational Course | CHP Training
The Three Pillars of Conveyor Motion

text_chunks.title: Why the Belt Drifts (Misalignment)
text_chunks.content: Why the Belt Drifts (Misalignment) The belt naturally tends to drift (wander sideways) if there is any asymmetry — uneven loading, idlers not perfectly perpendicular to belt travel, wind, or a bent frame. Even a slight drift accumulates over the length of the belt. If not corrected, the belt edge contacts the conveyor structure, causing edge damage, spillage, and ultimately belt failure. Self-aligning idlers and training idlers are used to correct drift automatically. A drifted belt that contacts the steel structure can generate enough heat through friction to ignite coal dust — causing a conveyor fire. Belt fires in CHP are a major risk and have caused plant outages lasting weeks.
breadcrumb: Belt Conveyor Operation – L1 Foundational Course | CHP Training

text_chunks.title: Conveyor Capacity & Throughput
text_chunks.content: Conveyor Capacity & Throughput Think of capacity as a "pipe size" — the pipe can carry only so much per second. Push more in than it can carry, and it overflows. Push less, and the plant is underfed. Every belt conveyor is designed to carry a specific maximum tonnage per hour (TPH) . This is called the rated capacity. The conveyor design — belt width, speed, inclination, and idler spacing — is optimised for this rated capacity. Operating at or above this limit causes problems; operating well below causes inefficiency.
breadcrumb: Belt Conveyor Operation – L1 Foundational Course | CHP Training

text_chunks.title: Factors That Determine Capacity
text_chunks.content: Factors That Determine Capacity Factor | How It Affects Capacity | Typical Values (CHP) ; Belt Width | Wider belt = larger cross-sectional area of coal = more tonnes per metre of belt. A wider belt also tolerates larger coal lumps. | 800 mm, 1000 mm, 1200 mm, 1400 mm ; Belt Speed | Higher speed moves the same cross-section faster → more TPH. But higher speed increases dust, wear, and impact at feed points. | 1.2 – 2.5 m/s (typical CHP); up to 4 m/s (high-capacity) ; Trough Angle | Steeper trough (e.g. 35° vs 20°) holds more coal per cross-section. Most CHP conveyors use 35° troughing. | 20°, 25°, 30°, 35°, 45° ; Coal Density & Moisture | Wet coal is heavier per volume → higher tonnage for same volume. However, wet fine coal also sticks to the belt (carryback) and blocks chutes. | Dry coal: ~800 kg/m³; Wet: 900–1000 kg/m³ ; Inclination Angle | Inclined conveyors carry less coal per hour than flat ones at the same belt speed (gravity opposes motion). Steep inclines also risk coal rolling back if belt speed drops. | Max practical: 15°–18° for coal; beyond this, cleated belts needed ; Feed Rate from Feeder | If the upstream feeder delivers more coal than the conveyor is rated for, the belt will be overloaded regardless of its rated capacity. | Controlled via feeder speed (variable frequency drive) When a conveyor is overloaded: (1) coal spills over the belt edges; (2) the motor draws excess current and may trip on overload protection; (3) the belt sags between idlers, increasing friction; (4) the drive may slip; (5) structural stress on the frame increases. Repeated overloading shortens belt life significantly. Underloading (running a conveyor almost empty) wastes electrical energy and accelerates belt wear due to the constant flexing of an unloaded belt over idlers. It also reduces the effective cleaning action of belt cleaners and increases dust generation from the empty belt vibrating on return idlers. A 500 MW thermal unit needs approximately 250–300 TPH of coal at full load. If the belt conveyor can carry 400 TPH rated capacity, there is a buffer. If an upstream crusher or feeder fails and reduces supply to 150 TPH, the bunker level gradually falls and load must be reduced. An intern does not control these rates — but understanding this relationship lets you understand the urgency when a supervisor responds to a falling bunker level.
breadcrumb: Belt Conveyor Operation – L1 Foundational Course | CHP Training

text_chunks.title: Transfer Points & Flow Behaviour
text_chunks.content: Transfer Points & Flow Behaviour A transfer point is like a controlled handover baton pass — coal must land precisely on the next belt. Any miss, blockage, or misalignment at this point disrupts the entire downstream flow. Wherever coal moves from one conveyor to the next — or from a hopper to a conveyor — there is a transfer point . These are not minor connections; they are among the most critical and most hazardous locations in the entire Coal Handling Plant. Understanding what happens at a transfer point is essential before entering the CHP. BC-1 (Upper Conveyor) Coal on BC-1 Head Pulley TRANSFER CHUTE (guides coal) ↓ Coal falls here BC-2 (Lower Conveyor) Impact Zone Coal on BC-2 ⚠ DUST ⚠ Spillage ⚠ Spillage ⚠ BLOCKAGE RISK Wet/sticky coal can block chute Coal must land centrally on BC-2 belt. Any deviation → spillage or belt drift.
