textchunk_objects.content: Overloading → Belt Stress → Spillage → Motor Trip Cause: The feeder speed is set too high, or a sudden surge from the wagon tippler overwhelms the hopper. Coal falls on the belt at a rate exceeding rated capacity. What Happens: Coal piles up on the belt, exceeding the trough capacity. Spillage occurs from both edges. The belt sags more between idlers, increasing rolling resistance. Motor current rises. Motor protection relay detects overload and trips the motor. The belt stops. Coal continues to fall from the hopper onto the stationary belt, burying it under a pile of coal. Early Signs: High motor current alarm. Increased spillage at feed point. Belt visibly overloaded (coal reaching edge of trough). Vibration increase. Consequence: Conveyor buried under coal. Manual digging-out required (hours of labour). Belt may be damaged under the weight. Entire coal flow stopped.

textchunk_objects.content: Poor Transfer Point Flow → Chute Blockage → System Shutdown Cause: Wet, fine coal (after rain or due to high moisture content) builds up on the inner walls of the transfer chute. Over time, coal bridges across the chute opening. What Happens: Coal flow through the chute reduces, then stops. BC-1 continues running — coal piles up at the head pulley discharge point and overflows the chute. BC-2 runs empty, drawing coal from the bunker without being replenished. Bunker level falls. Eventually, BC-1 is tripped on overload as coal piles up. The plant is called to reduce load. Early Signs: BC-2 belt running empty (visible drop in load current). Spillage at base of transfer chute. Unusual noise from chute (hollow sound instead of coal flow sound). Consequence: Manual chute cleaning required. Confined space permit needed. Risk of coal avalanche when blockage suddenly clears.

textchunk_objects.content: Belt Slipping on Drive Pulley → Loss of Conveying → Overheating Cause: Water or coal slurry contaminates the surface of the drive pulley, reducing friction. Or the take-up tension is insufficient. The belt cannot maintain grip on the rotating pulley. What Happens: The drive pulley continues to rotate, but the belt slips — moving slower than the pulley surface. This generates significant heat at the pulley-belt contact zone. The rubber lagging on the pulley begins to burn. Acrid smoke is generated. If the conveyor is not stopped, the lagging is destroyed, and eventually the belt itself can ignite. Meanwhile, coal stops moving because the belt is stationary or barely moving. Early Signs: Burning rubber smell. Smoke from head end. Reduced belt speed indicator. High motor current (motor is working hard but belt is not moving at designed speed). Consequence: Belt fire — major safety incident. Drive pulley lagging replacement. Potential partial belt damage. 1–3 days outage.

textchunk_objects.content: Dust Accumulation Ignition → Conveyor Fire Cause: Coal dust accumulates on conveyor structure, idlers, and the underside of the belt over weeks without adequate housekeeping. A seized idler generates frictional heat. This heat ignites the accumulated coal dust. What Happens: Smouldering begins on the structure or inside the belt tunnel. Because coal dust is distributed over a large area, the fire can spread rapidly along the full length of the conveyor. In an enclosed conveyor (gallery), fire and smoke can develop quickly. A conveyor fire can destroy the entire belt (hundreds of metres long), the structure, and adjacent equipment. Early Signs: Burning smell. Smoke in the conveyor gallery. Seized idler (idler not rotating despite belt moving — creates a flat worn spot on the idler and local heating). Unusual hotspot detected by thermal camera. Consequence: Major fire incident. Full belt replacement. Structural repairs. Plant outage of weeks. Regulatory investigation. Possible fatalities if personnel are in the gallery.

textchunk_objects.content: Exposure to Moving Parts → Entanglement Injury Cause: A person reaches over or near a running conveyor without adequate clearance. Loose clothing, gloves, or hair contacts the moving belt or a rotating idler/pulley. What Happens: The belt instantly grips the material and draws the person's limb or clothing into the nip point. At 1.5 m/s belt speed and with a motor delivering hundreds of kilowatts, the force is thousands of times greater than human strength. No one can pull free. The injury is instantaneous and typically irreversible — degloving, crush, amputation, or fatal entrapment. Prevention: Guard all nip points (mandatory, not optional). Never approach a running conveyor without proper authorisation. Emergency pull cord must be functional and tested. Buddy system — never work alone near running equipment. Consequence: Serious injury or fatality. Plant shutdown for investigation. Management liability. Irreparable human loss. There is zero tolerance in a professional plant for bypassing guards, reaching over running conveyors, or working near running equipment without proper PPE and procedures. This is not bureaucracy — it is the direct lesson from real fatalities.

textchunk_objects.content: You Are L1-Ready When You Can… A trainee is considered ready for site induction (L1 complete) when they can demonstrate the following outcomes — not just recall them, but explain them in their own words to a senior engineer: End-to-End Coal Flow: Clearly explain how coal travels from the railway wagon through the wagon tippler, hopper, feeder, conveyors, transfer points, and finally into the bunker and boiler — and what each stage depends on. Component Identification: Walk along a conveyor and correctly name and describe the function of the belt, drive pulley, tail pulley, idlers, take-up system, scrapers, feed point, and all guards and safety devices. Mechanism Understanding: Explain how motion is generated (motor → gearbox → drive pulley → friction → belt), why tension is critical, how idlers support the belt, and why belt drift occurs and is dangerous. Capacity Awareness: Explain the factors that affect conveyor capacity (belt width, speed, inclination, coal density), what overloading and underloading look like, and why both are problematic for the plant. Hazard Identification: Point to and describe every high-risk zone on a conveyor (pinch points, moving belt, transfer points, dust zones), explain the associated injury types, and correctly identify the emergency pull cord and its purpose. Failure Consequence Awareness: Describe at least 4 failure scenarios, their early warning signs, and their consequences for plant continuity, machinery integrity, and human safety — without reading from notes.

textchunk_objects.content: Instrumentation & Safety Devices on the Conveyor Think of instrumentation as the conveyor's nervous system — sensors spread across the full length that continuously sense abnormal conditions and either warn operators or automatically stop the machine before a small problem becomes a catastrophe. A belt conveyor in a modern Coal Handling Plant is fitted with numerous sensors, switches, and protective devices along its entire length. These are not optional extras — they are mandatory safety and operational requirements under Indian Electricity Rules, factory safety regulations, and plant operating procedures. As an intern, you will see these devices everywhere on the conveyor. Knowing what each one does is essential. textchunk_objects.content: Safety Device Reference Guide Device | Location on Conveyor | Function | Response When Activated ; Emergency Pull Cord (EPC) | Both sides, full length of conveyor, approximately every 30–50 m | Allows any person anywhere along the conveyor to immediately stop it in an emergency by pulling the rope/wire | Immediate emergency stop of conveyor drive motor. Conveyor cannot restart until EPC is reset and root cause investigated. ; Belt Sway Switch (BSW) | Both sides, spaced every 50–75 m along carry and return strand | Detects lateral drift of the belt beyond a set limit. Has two positions: first position = alarm; second position = trip. | First activation: Alarm in control room. Second (greater drift): Conveyor trip. Prevents belt edge from contacting steel structure. ; Zero Speed Switch (ZSS) | Tail pulley shaft or on a return idler | Monitors belt speed. Detects if the belt has stopped (zero speed) while the motor is still running — indicating belt slip. | Conveyor trip + alarm. Prevents drive pulley from running against a stationary belt (which causes fire from friction). ; Belt Weigher (BW) | Fixed location on the conveyor, typically mid-span | Measures the weight of coal on the belt per unit length using load cells. Calculates instantaneous TPH and cumulative tonnes. | Data sent to control room / DCS. No trip — provides operational data. High load may trigger an alarm. ; Chute Blocked Detector (CBD) | Inside transfer chutes at transfer points | Detects when coal has accumulated and blocked the chute (using vibration probe, ultrasonic, or paddle switch). | Alarm in control room. May automatically stop upstream feeder to prevent further coal accumulation. ; Thermal / Fire Detector | Inside conveyor galleries (tunnels) and transfer towers | Detects elevated temperature indicating a developing fire. Linear heat detection cable runs along the belt gallery roof. | Fire alarm. Conveyor trip. Activation of fire suppression system (CO₂ or water mist). Control room alert. ; Underspeed Switch | Drive shaft area | Detects if belt is running slower than designed speed (but not zero). Indicates overloading or drive slip developing. | Alarm → trip if underspeed persists. Allows early intervention before full slippage occurs. ; Motor Overload Relay (OLR) | Motor control centre (MCC) / switchgear panel | Monitors motor current. If the motor draws current above the rated limit for a set time (indicating overload), it trips. | Motor trip + alarm. Conveyor stops. Investigation required to identify overload cause before restart. When you walk a conveyor on site, you will see red ropes, yellow boxes, and small switches mounted on the frame at regular intervals — these are all part of this safety system. You will hear terms like "BSW trip," "ZSS alarm," or "EPC activation" on the radio constantly. Now you know exactly what each term means, what triggered it, and what the plant team needs to do in response. On some plants, under production pressure, well-meaning but incorrect actions include bypassing a belt sway switch that keeps tripping, disabling a chute blocked detector that gives "false" alarms, or tying off an EPC that was accidentally pulled. This is an extremely dangerous practice. Every safety device bypass removes one layer of protection from the system. Multiple bypasses create a condition where a fatal accident can occur without any warning. As an intern, if you are ever asked to bypass a safety device, immediately consult your supervisor. Document it. Never accept it as routine.

textchunk_objects.content: Your First Site Visit – What to Observe & What to Look For Your first site visit is not a tour — it is a structured observation exercise. For every component you studied in this course, there is a physical object in front of you. Treat it like matching a textbook diagram to a real machine, component by component. Now that you understand the system theoretically, you need to translate that knowledge to what you will actually see, hear, and smell when you walk into the Coal Handling Plant for the first time. This guide prepares you for that transition, so you do not feel overwhelmed or miss important details. Site Visit Observation Sequence – Walk the Conveyor Like an Engineer STEP 1 Start at the Feed Point (Tail End) Observe loading STEP 2 Walk Along One Side of Belt Check belt & idlers STEP 3 Observe Drive / Head End Check discharge STEP 4 Look at Safety Devices EPC, sway switches STEP 5 Visit Transfer Tower (outside) Observe from safe zone STEP 6 – REFLECT & REPORT Note all abnormalities observed. Discuss with supervisor. NEVER act on abnormalities independently. ⛔ NEVER do this on your first visit: Do not touch, adjust, or interfere with any equipment — observe only.

textchunk_objects.content: Step-by-Step: What to Look For at Each Location Location | What a Healthy System Looks Like | Warning Signs to Report ; Feed Point (Tail End) | Coal lands centrally on the belt. Skirt boards are close to the belt surface with no visible gap. No coal spillage outside the belt edges. Dust suppression sprays (if fitted) are operating. | Coal spilling over belt edges. Gap between skirt board and belt. Coal piling up at sides. Dust cloud larger than usual. Unusual impact noise from large lumps. ; Belt Surface (While Walking Alongside) | Belt is centred on idlers. Surface is intact — no cuts, gouges, or longitudinal slits. Coal is uniformly distributed across the belt width. Belt moves smoothly without lateral wandering. | Belt visibly off-centre (drift). Belt edge near or touching structure. Cuts or rips on belt surface. Uneven coal load (all on one side). Belt flapping or vibrating excessively. ; Idlers (Along the Full Length) | All idlers are spinning freely as the belt passes over them. No noise from any individual idler. No flat spot on any roller (from seizure). All idlers are in their correct mounting position. | Any idler NOT spinning (seized — belt slides over it creating heat). Grinding or squealing noise from an idler bearing. Idler shell worn flat on one spot. Idler hanging loose or displaced from its bracket. ; Structure & Walkway (Below the Belt) | Walkway is clean — minimal coal spillage on the floor. Structure is intact. No coal accumulated on structural members. Return strand is clean (minimal carryback coal on the underside). | Coal accumulated on structural members (fire risk). Excessive carryback falling onto the floor below. Wet coal mix on walkway (slip hazard). Smell of burning rubber or coal smoke. ; Drive / Head End | Coal discharges cleanly over the head pulley into the chute. Belt scraper is in contact with the belt and removing carryback. Head pulley guard is in place. No burning smell. Motor noise is normal (steady hum). | Coal not discharging cleanly (flying off sideways). Burning rubber smell (belt slipping on pulley). Unusual motor noise (overload — grinding or laboured hum). Scraper not in contact with belt. Any guard missing. ; Safety Devices | All EPC ropes are present, unbroken, and at the correct tension (not sagging to ground, not over-tight). Belt sway switches are mounted and free. No safety device is taped up, bypassed, or disabled. | EPC rope broken, missing, or sagging. Sway switch blocked with coal or debris. Any safety device with a bypass tag or wire tied in bypassed position. Missing nip point guards at pulleys. ; Transfer Tower (from outside / entrance) | Coal flow sound is continuous and steady from inside (not intermittent). No coal spillage on the outside of the tower base. Dust seal curtains at openings are intact. | Silence from chute (blockage). Coal spilling from tower base. Dust escaping from every gap (excess spillage inside). Unusual vibration of the tower structure. As an intern, you will not be allowed to operate equipment. But you can walk the conveyors during your inspection rounds with a supervisor, and you can see things that busy operators may have overlooked . A fresh pair of eyes — trained by this course to know what is normal and what is not — can catch an early warning sign that prevents a major failure. Always report what you observe to your supervisor, and never assume "someone else must have seen it already."

These are not rules imposed on you — they are the behaviours that keep you alive and healthy during your internship and throughout your career in the power industry.

Do's and Don'ts for the Intern in the Coal Handling Plant

textchunk_objects.content: ✅ DO – Always ✔ Always wear your complete PPE before entering the CHP area — helmet, boots, high-vis vest, and dust mask at minimum. ✔ Always stay on designated walkways. Never take shortcuts across structural members or below return strands. ✔ Always walk in pairs (buddy system) inside CHP, especially in galleries and near transfer towers. ✔ Always report abnormalities (seized idler, missing guard, damaged EPC) to your supervisor immediately — verbally and in writing. ✔ Always ask for a proper explanation before approaching any equipment you have not previously been briefed on. ✔ Always maintain a minimum clearance of 1 metre from the belt and moving machinery unless you are following a supervised inspection protocol. ✔ Always wear close-fitting clothing. Tuck in shirts. No loose ties, scarves, or dangling lanyards. ✔ Always know the location of the nearest Emergency Pull Cord and fire extinguisher on any conveyor you are walking. ✔ Always pull the EPC without hesitation if you see an entanglement, smoke, or fire — never wait for confirmation.

textchunk_objects.content: ⛔ DON'T – Never ✘ Never touch a moving belt — not to feel the speed, test the surface, or remove a piece of coal from it. ✘ Never lean over a running conveyor for any reason — not to look at the other side, not to pick up a fallen object. ✘ Never attempt to clear a blocked chute or dislodged coal from a running conveyor using your hands, feet, or tools. ✘ Never remove guards from pulleys or other rotating parts — even "just to check" something. ✘ Never silence or bypass a safety alarm without a supervisor's explicit authorisation and a proper investigation. ✘ Never enter a transfer tower, conveyor gallery, or any confined space without a valid Confined Space Entry Permit. ✘ Never operate any switch, valve, or control on the conveyor unless specifically instructed and supervised by an authorised engineer. ✘ Never work alone in the CHP — especially in conveyor galleries, transfer towers, and tunnels below trestle conveyors. ✘ Never assume a stopped conveyor is safe without confirming it is Locked Out / Tagged Out (LOTO) by a qualified person. One of the most common causes of serious injury in industrial plants is working on equipment that appears to be stopped but is not properly isolated. A conveyor belt that stopped due to an alarm can be restarted from the control room while someone is working on it. The Lockout-Tagout (LOTO) procedure requires the drive to be electrically isolated at the switchgear, locked with a physical padlock, and tagged with the worker's identity before any maintenance work begins. As an intern, you must never approach any equipment for maintenance purposes. If asked to, immediately request that proper LOTO isolation is carried out and confirmed before you go near the equipment.

textchunk_objects.content: Glossary of CHP & Belt Conveyor Terms On your first day on site you will hear these terms constantly. This glossary ensures you are not lost in the conversation. Term | Meaning ; Belt | The continuous rubber-fabric loop that carries coal from tail to head end. ; Belt Conveyor (BC) | The complete conveyor assembly — numbered in sequence (BC-1, BC-2, etc.) in the plant. ; Carry Strand | The top run of the belt that carries coal toward the discharge point. ; Return Strand | The lower run of the empty belt going back from head to tail. ; Head Pulley | The drive pulley at the discharge end of the conveyor. ; Tail Pulley | The non-driven pulley at the loading end. ; Idler | A free-spinning roller that supports the belt. Troughing idlers (carry) and flat idlers (return). ; Trough Angle | The angle at which wing idler rolls are tilted to form the trough (20°–45°). ; Take-up | The tensioning device — gravity, screw, or hydraulic — that keeps the belt at correct tension. ; Lagging | Rubber coating on the drive pulley surface to increase friction with the belt. ; Skirt Board | Side rubber/steel walls at the feed point that contain coal on the belt edge. ; Scraper / Cleaner | A blade pressed against the belt at the head end to remove carryback coal. ; Carryback | Fine coal that sticks to the belt after discharge and is carried back on the return strand. ; Transfer Point | Location where coal moves from one conveyor to the next via a chute. ; Chute | The steel guide structure that directs coal from one conveyor to the next at transfer points. ; Tripper Car | A movable discharge device on a conveyor above the bunker that distributes coal across bunker bays. Term | Meaning ; Bunker | Large coal storage silo above the boiler, fed by the conveyor. Buffer for continuous boiler feeding. ; Hopper | A funnel-shaped collection vessel below the wagon tippler that collects unloaded coal. ; Feeder | A device (vibrating, apron, or belt type) that controls the rate of coal feeding onto the conveyor. ; TPH | Tonnes Per Hour — the standard unit of conveyor throughput capacity. ; CHP | Coal Handling Plant — the entire system for receiving, processing, and conveying coal in a power plant. ; DCS | Distributed Control System — the central computerised control system monitoring all CHP parameters. ; MCC | Motor Control Centre — the electrical switchgear panel that starts, stops, and protects conveyor motors. ; EPC | Emergency Pull Cord — the safety rope running the full length of the conveyor for emergency stop. ; BSW | Belt Sway Switch — sensor that detects lateral belt drift and triggers alarm/trip. ; ZSS / USS | Zero Speed Switch / Underspeed Switch — detects belt slippage or stall. ; LOTO | Lockout-Tagout — energy isolation procedure before maintenance on conveyor or any equipment. ; Nip Point | The point where the belt meets a pulley — the most dangerous entanglement zone. ; Belt Drift | Lateral wandering of the belt off centre — can cause edge damage and fire. ; Tight Side | The belt strand leaving the drive pulley (carry side) — where belt tension is highest. ; Slack Side | The belt strand returning to the drive pulley — where tension is lower. ; CWP | Coal Workers' Pneumoconiosis — lung disease caused by long-term coal dust inhalation ("black lung").
